Where it began

Dilip Vengsarkar was born in Rajapur on 6 April 1956 and went to school at Raja Shivaji Vidyalaya. He made his Test debut at Auckland in 1976, against New Zealand, as an opener. India won that match comfortably, though he made few runs himself. Before long he found his true home lower down, at number three or four.

The player

He played 116 Tests between 1976 and 1992, scoring 6,868 runs at 42.13 with 17 hundreds and 35 fifties. He also held 78 catches. For years he sat in the middle of a strong Indian order alongside Sunil Gavaskar and Gundappa Viswanath.

The innings many remember came at Delhi in 1979. India needed 390 to win on the last day, and Vengsarkar carried the chase almost all the way. With partners running out he settled for a draw, unbeaten on 146, and India finished just 26 short. In the 1978–79 series against the West Indies he had shared a stand of more than 300 with Gavaskar at Calcutta.

He was part of the side that won the 1983 World Cup and the team that won the World Championship of Cricket in 1985. Between 1985 and 1987 he made hundreds against five different countries, and for a spell of 21 months he sat at the top of the world batting ratings. He later captained India in 10 Tests, starting with two hundreds in his first series in charge, and led them to the Asia Cup in 1988.

What made him special

His driving was the thing, and it was a pleasure to watch. He was also one of the few batsmen of his time who could cope with the great West Indian fast bowlers, and made six hundreds against them.

He loved Lord's. When he made a hundred there in 1986, it was his third in three Test matches at the ground. His bowling was a different story: he did turn his arm over in Tests, but the wicket never came, and nobody seems to have held it against him.

Away from the middle

India gave him the Arjuna Award in 1981 and the Padma Shri in 1987, the year Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year. The board later honoured him with its C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award in 2014.

After his playing days he gave a great deal back. He founded the Elf-Vengsarkar Academy in 1995 and went on to run academies in Mumbai and Pune that coach selected young players free of charge. He served as vice-president of the Mumbai Cricket Association, led the board's talent development wing when it was set up, and was chairman of India's selectors.

And finally

In the 2021 film 83, about India's first World Cup win, he was played by Adinath Kothare. Not many batsmen get to see themselves played on the big screen. For a man with three Lord's hundreds in a row, a starring role seems only fair.
